utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to all. May we begin in the usual manner by having the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Gramsci De Fazio, Joanna Korner, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan for the Defence of Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Zupljanin Defence Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and Jason Antley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Court dictated that we adjourn before a matter which had been raised by Mr. O'Sullivan and responded to, I believe by Ms. Korner, on behalf of the Prosecution had been definitively resolved. Unless either side feels some burning need to make further submissions to the Chamber, we think we have an appreciation of what is in dispute between the parties, but we are not prepared to give our ruling at this point. It's something that we would wish to consider and the -- as soon as we have concretised the position that we take on this, we would give an indication. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the burning need, I shall say, is, at the moment we are in a position where if you are not going to rule on the admission of Mr. Draganovic's testimony as an exhibit, plus the documents that accompany it, where are we if it's not going to be admitted? I don't think it's - with the greatest of respect Your Honours - I don't think it's something you can delay, because if it's not admitted then he has to be called in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsels, the reason why we wanted time to consider the issue that was brought up by Mr. O'Sullivan yesterday is that we wanted to consider carefully the implications of Rule 92 ter, because the rule doesn't set out clearly what exactly the Prosecution is supposed to do in these cases. It's obvious that when we deal with Rule 92 bis, that is to say in situations where the witness is not coming, in those situations it seems incumbent on the Prosecution to bring all documents, not only Prosecution documents but also documents introduced by the Defence that are adjacent to the testimonies that's come in through 92 bis. But then what is the situation in respect of Rule 92 ter? There we could either choose to say, well, in the cases of 92 ter, the same mechanism applies, the Prosecution has to bring both Defence and Prosecution documents. However, Rule 92 ter really doesn't imply this because obviously here the witness is brought for cross-examination. So that's why we were hesitant to set out the principle because we need to discuss it more thoroughly. But for the moment, what we will say is that in respect of this witness, his testimony is admitted and along with it the 92 ter package that the Prosecution has proposed. We are then confident that for this witness, the Defence will then be free to advance the documents that are adjacent to these testimonies and that were once introduced through the Defence counsels in the other cases. So for this witness, we will just go along the way the Prosecution has proposed and we will then reserve our position on what to do in future cases. So for this witness, Mr. O'Sullivan, we kindly ask you to identify those documents that you wish to have introduced and then, as I said, we'll get back with a more principled decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And may I add that, of course, as I indicated yesterday, what comes in, in evidence from the transcripts will only be the parts that have been highlighted by the Prosecution. That goes without saying. It goes for all the 92 ter testimonies. And, of course, the documents that come in are only the documents that are related to those highlighted part of the transcripts. I think this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's news to us. That's the first time you've said that. We've highlighted -- we've -- so far and that's the way the motion was drafted and acceded to by Your Honours' ruling. We have highlighted -- we put in all the transcript but highlighted the parts that we thought were relevant, where it it's very long transcript as it was in this case. So the whole of the transcript is admitted. If it's not, none of the cross-examination from this would be highlighted because we don't -- or not -- or very little of it because we didn't consider it was relevant. So it's got to be -- and that's the way the motions are drafted and that's the ruling. The prior -- it's not partial transcript, it's the prior transcripts, full stop. So it has to be the whole transcript with the highlighting as an indication of what you should consider to be relevant, and obviously we've selected the documents that we considered to be relevant, and indeed Your Honours, as I say, made a considerable effort with this witness because in paragraph 15 of your ruling of the 2nd of October you say: "The Trial Chamber in its review of the accompanying documents finds that most of them do indeed form an inextricable and indispensable part of the evidence they accompany, save for the involving ..." And then literally there is a page and a half of documents which you listed which you didn't consider to be relevant and which we removed, out of what we had already selected. So with the greatest of respect, Your Honours, it has to be the whole transcript plus the documents that you admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As far as we were able to establish, the documents that you have proposed now to come in along with the testimony, they do only relate to the highlighted parts, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would hope so, yes. I imagine so. I must say, it's not an exercise I've gone back to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we checked and we discovered --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can see Judge Delvoie nodding. So they do, yes, they do. But the whole transcript has to go in as an exhibit. Not just -- I mean, otherwise you've got -- you are going to chop around with the transcript which may not make sense as to what it's leading into, if you see what I mean. And also, as I say, it would exclude the Defence part because that's -- we didn't highlight it as particularly relevant. So, as I say, Your Honours, I think it has to be the whole transcript, and that's what we have understood your rulings to be. Your Honours, Mr. Smith has pulled up our original motion, and we say effectively that it's a long -- we ask for the whole transcript to be admitted, but because it's a long one, we've highlighted the relevant parts, and your ruling simply said the transcript. It was the 27th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It seems as if this is subject to all sorts of interesting interpretations. If we allow the entire testimony to go in, then we will only pay attention and have regard to the highlighted parts, so you know, whichever way you want to put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you see the Defence, Your Honour, I think that's it. The Defence may want to draw attention to other parts of the transcript, so you have to admitted the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, no, they are free to draw to our attention the parts that they want to highlight. This whole exercise was made in an attempt to shorten the amount of evidence that comes in. And so to focus and to narrow down on the parts that are really relevant so that we can disregard the rest. This is an ongoing struggle by this Chamber to seek to narrow down the scope of the evidence to what is really essential and necessary and relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that. I don't think, however, that you are causing yourself any problem by this. You admit the transcript. We've highlighted the parts we think are relevant. The Defence can draw your attention to the other parts that they think are relevant, but the transcript is there as an exhibit. And moreover, you never know what is going to happen in the future. It may well be that as a result of what happens in the trial other parts of that transcript may become relevant, so therefore you admit the transcript but you only look at the parts that are highlighted, simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, isn't it a little bit like you want to draw the Court's attention to three pages out of a book, and if you hand over materially the book, you hand over the book, not only the three pages, you don't tear out the three pages, but it's more or less that. But the only thing that goes in is what you said that has to go in, three pages of the book, and not then the book in the whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I say this, it's not quite the same thing as a book, because a book is divided into chapters. These transcripts are a continuation of a witness telling the -- giving his account of what happened. Although only certain parts may be particularly relevant, none of it is irrelevant as such. I mean, you can't really say it's completely irrelevant to any issue in this case, the whole of judge Draganovic's testimony is relevant to issues that arise in this case, but there are particular portions which relate particularly, for example, in this case to the actions of the MUP, and it is those that we have highlighted. And that's the -- all other matters that go to the question of joint criminal enterprise, but those are the matters we've highlighted, but you can't say it's irrelevant, as such. And that's literally what I'm -- I am sorry Mr. O'Sullivan, just let me finish. That is literally what our motion said, and your ruling hasn't been, and indeed nor am I aware of any other Trial Chamber's ruling that has been to that effect where this section has been used of the rules, that only the highlighted parts are admitted. The rulings in all, as far as I am aware of, I know of no ruling any Trial Chamber where it's simply been the highlighted part that is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There are with respect a number of points here which are important, we submit. Now, Rule 92 ter provides that in lieu of having the witness testify viva voce as a time-saving mechanism, 800 pages of previous transcript can come into evidence. And your ruling on the 2nd of October, I'm looking at paragraph 12, where you identify two witness, ST-155 and ST-198 as being irrelevant and therefore inadmissible, and all the other 33 that the Prosecution tendered you admit the entire transcript as being relevant. Now, when it comes to what the parties do eventually with any of this evidence is for final submission or submission on the evidence. The Prosecution may only rely on a certain pages of the 800 pages, and we may only rely on certain segments, but that's further down the road. At this point if the transcripts are admitted as they are, and if your ruling is that associated documents are necessary to be able to make submission, we may say that person is not credible because in cross-examination in a previous trial, he was shown exhibits -- Defence exhibits 1, 2, 3 from the previous trial, and we say don't believe him, he is a liar, you need to see those exhibits from the previous trial, so they must be in this case. So in the final analysis, it's -- at the point of final submission where the parties will choose the evidence on which they rely to persuade you, one way or the other, but those pieces of the puzzle must be admitted, the transcript and the associated documents. And it's different than a book, Your Honour, in this sense. In fact your guide-lines on the book say that a book, the relevant pages of a book may come in, and it may be a concise controlled package, it may be. A transcript is different. This is this -- these people's -- witness's testimony is in fact the direct, the cross-examination, and judges questions from those previous proceedings, and we need to have that to be able to make submission to you in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Counsel, prudence dictates that we adjourn now so that we can give you guide-lines by way of a ruling before we proceed further with the witness who isn't present in the box.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I just say this, with the greatest of respect, you've ruled, and we have proceeded on the basis of of this ruling. And to suddenly change the whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is precisely why I began by saying prudence dictates. We are aware that we have ruled on this matter, and we do not -- we wouldn't take a position that is inconsistent with that ruling. But we don't want to be placed in a position of having to further clarify what we thought had been clarified earlier. You want to assist, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One final matter in relation to that is our request for consideration of the 9th of October. Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If counsel has deduced that our delay in resuming in taking the Bench again was due to the complications of this issue, they are correct. Judge Harhoff will give our conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber's ruling is the following: The testimony of this witness and of 92 ter witnesses in the future are admitted in their entirety. The Prosecution is required to highlight the parts of the testimony that they wish to draw particularly attention to, and they are required also to select the relevant documents that were admitted into evidence in the previous trials through the parts that have been highlighted. The Defence is free to put to the witness any other document that was admitted through this witness in the earlier testimony, and they are thus not limited to only using the documents that have been selected through the -- through the selection made by the Prosecution. We think this decision is in conformity with the Chamber's earlier ruling of 2nd October, and we are ready to proceed from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just to make sure we've understood, in regard to the Defence, if a document has been put to the witness in the previous trial, there's no need for us to do this again, is there? He has already testified about a previous document, it seems that 92 ter is designed to save court time and not to have us repeat an exercise that has been done. In relation to this witness he was cross-examined for three and a half days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, the purpose of this exercise, you will recall, is to narrow down the scope of the evidence that comes in. We can do this in various ways. As far as the Prosecution is concerned, because they are waiving the right to examine in chief by choosing to introduce this witness through 92 ter, we are requiring the Prosecution to identify those documents that they seek to have admitted along with the testimony. The Defence still has the freedom of cross-examining. Now, if the Defence were allowed to just insist that all documents introduced through this witness in the earlier trial were to be admitted, then that would defeat the purpose of Rule 92 ter and would certainly defeat the struggle that this Chamber is trying to have in order to limit the evidence to what is necessary and relevant. That's why the Chamber thinks that if the Defence wishes to have a particular document introduced into evidence and admitted into evidence in this trial, then they have to put it to the witness. Just as they would have to do it in any other cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are certainly not prepared to proceed on that basis. We haven't prepared the cross-examination of this witness or any other 92 bis [sic] witness on that basis. The assumption has been, your rulings have been, that the -- well, Your Honour, yes, we are suffering great prejudice if we have to decide by noon today which of the three and a half days of testimony from Brdjanin documents which are -- which we may not even have access to at this point on the basis of your ruling today after two months of trial. That puts us in a very serious position. Tremendous burden. The position is that in lieu of having this man come for 11 days, which he could have come for 11 days had he been viva voce, in which case there would have been a complete repetition of what Ms. Korner asked him and what the Defence would have put to him if he were viva voce. He is not, he is 92 ter, and that he has adopted his 92 ter transcripts as giving -- he would give the same answers here as he did several years ago. And that's the basis for his admission of his testimony, and our cross-examination is not necessary, it's a time saving device. Please don't put the emphasis on reducing the scope of the number of exhibits. That's unfair to us. We have assumed that what he was cross-examined on in Talic and Brdjanin is the basis for the truth and relevance of what he will -- has adopted yesterday in this court. And it's a time-wasting exercise to even go through the process of showing him the same documents that were used by the Defence in the previous trial. Not to mention the fact that we are not in a position to do that. And I believe what I'm recounting here is completely consistent with the practice of this Tribunal in all previous cases under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does 92 ter say that the prior testimony and evidence can be admitted in whole or in part?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With respect, that is not what it says. It says that the evidence of the witness may be in whole or in part his previous testimony. This is what I mean. The witness can adopt his previous testimony, the statement of the transcript, and say I would answer the same way today as I did then. And there can be no further questions from the Prosecution. His evidence is in whole, his previous statement. It can be in whole or in part because then he can be asked further questions as has been done here. So once the previous statement or transcript is admitted, if in fact we take it one step further, Judge Delvoie, we've seen witnesses correct, bring modifications to their previous statement, which again suggests that that is his testimony then or is his evidence -- under 29 ter, his evidence, then, is the previous statement plus the corrections he made in court. And typically there's no need for any further questions unless the party calling that witness determines that they want to add additional questions. So the phrase in whole or in part refers to his evidence, which may be in whole, that statement; or in part, oral and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, there has to be a reasonable and a practical way of doing this. If your suggestion is that each and every document admitted into evidence in the earlier trial through this witness must come in and also be admitted into evidence in this trial, then I think that you are asking for a lot more than you really need. You see that the Chamber is requiring from the Prosecution to identify the documents that they wish to have admitted along with the testimony. That would make no sense if we were to follow your suggestion, namely that all documents come in. So this is why the Chamber is of the view that there has to be a way in which the Defence can indicate which documents they wish to have admitted. We can ask you to put forward a list as we are asking the Prosecution to do, but I don't see the need to have each and every document which may be totally irrelevant to this case admitted into evidence just because of the fact that it was admitted in the previous trial. So please be helpful, if I may put it this way, and come forward with some sort of a solution by which we can take into consideration and admit into evidence those documents that you seek to have admitted without necessarily having to put them to the witness. I can only see one solution, and that is to say give us a list and we'll admit those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll certainly address your specific question, but am I to assume that you have rejected our motion for reconsideration, which we say is the proper position, as you, yourself, as pre-trial judge and pre-trial Chamber said, only those exhibits on the 65 ter list are admissible? And that was precisely your first ruling on the 30th of September in relation to a 92 ter witness. If it's not on the exhibit list, it doesn't come in. Then on the 2nd of October your written decision said something different, absolutely. And since early October the Prosecution has been tendering many more documents that were not on the pre-trial brief 65 ter list. And that is the prejudice to us. We say, if you want to narrow the scope of the exhibits, we ask you to follow your pre-trial ruling which made it clear that we would be put on notice of the 65 ter list. Now, if with your going to -- that's the practical solution, we say. But if you are going to go the other way, as you did in -- on October 2nd, where you've determined which exhibits -- which prior statements and transcripts are relevant, then we say -- and in fact, if I can just refer you to that decision on the 2nd of October, at paragraph 16, you say, "In keeping with the jurisprudence of the other previous cases." And you refer to a number about the admission of relevant exhibits which are inseparable from the testimony of the witness. And they are inseparable from the testimony of the witness. If, for example, we want to make submission eventually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are beating around the bush, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, how can we argue the case if we don't have the relevant evidence, if only part of the relevance, only the testimony is there, and not the document to support a position that either party may wish to make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There is an underlying requirement of relevance and probative value and that has to be on -- that has to be the priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I quite agree. If during cross-examination under Rule 90 H, there are -- if the cross-examination was permitted in the Brdjanin trial, we have to assume that the Bench was able to determine that the questions put by counsel during that cross-examination was relative and probative, and therefore this man has said, This is my testimony. You are putting us in a terrible bind by not allowing us in the end to make submission because we will not have the basis to say you should not believe this person - I'll give one example - because in a previous trial he was shown a document Exhibit 2D of the Brdjanin case, which isn't in our case, if we follow what you are suggesting. There's no burden on the Chamber to admit the documents. The parties will decide in due course which aspects of the testimony we adopt. I don't see -- with all due respect, I don't see a difference between the 92 ter and actually having this witness testify viva voce for 11 days. Assume he did testify for 11 days, and the result was the transcript of the Brdjanin case, all that testimony and all those exhibits would be in, and we would deal with those accordingly in submission. And there's no court time wasted by using 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, no two trials are alike, and there will inevitably and necessarily be large parts of one trial that are irrelevant to the next trial. The Chamber is not seeking to prevent the Defence from anything. The Chamber is asking for your assistance to try and narrow down the scope of the evidence that is admitted into this trial. And if I may say, your suggestion that for this purpose each and every document that has been admitted in a prior trial must therefore also be admitted into evidence in this trial is neither helpful nor necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, if I can echo what Ms. Korner said earlier, we do not know at this point to what extent the evidence may become relevant because there are twists and turns in this trial which may not follow Krajisnik, Brdjanin, Milosevic. And this person -- we are relying on what the -- the parties are relying on the testimony of this person, for better or for worse on either side. In the end we may have to deal with that. Now, Your Honour, if the solution is to say because this is our position, we think that the cross-examination of this witness is relevant, we do, and we can provide you, I suppose we can go -- we can troll through the Brdjanin transcript and say, Here are the exhibits that counsel for Talic and Brdjanin used, and we don't have any questions on it, but we want you to have those documents so that when you read and we make submission on those -- that testimony, that you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can't you see -- I am sorry, I'll wait for the translation. In my view what you are asking is that you want the Chamber to do the work that is really to be done by the parties. You are asking us to troll through all the evidence that came in, in another trial, and then it's for us to select what we might find is relevant. And I'm sorry, my understanding is that this is the job of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That's what I'm saying. We're not asking you to -- you've ruled that the transcripts are admissible based on a motion filed by the Prosecution and a response by the Defence. We are not asking to you troll through the transcripts at all. The parties will make submissions in due course, perhaps at 98 bis, perhaps at the end of the case. And the parties will present to you what they say are the important aspects of all the evidence. So you are not having to go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And then -- I'll wait for the translation. And then why is it that we cannot ask the Defence to present us with a list of the adjacent documents that you wish to have admitted into this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we can, but our position will be -- our position will be, all of them. Our position will be all. That's precisely our point. Because we do not think it's fair to us to be unable -- at the end of the day to not be able to make a submission on the testimony of a witness who is speaking to a document from a previous trial that is not in evidence in ours. Because that's exactly what the consequence will be. We'll say witness X said this and here is his interpretation of the document, which may be beneficial to the Defence - we can't make that submission because you don't have the document in evidence. Or we can say, Don't believe this witness, and again there's no basis for us to say that because you have no way to evaluate our submission and our interpretation of what he said, which may be based on a document. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If you make that submission it goes without saying that the underlying document will be admitted into evidence here as well. It's not that difficult. What I'm trying to weed out is only the documents that have no importance, no bearing on anything that the witness said during his cross-examination in the earlier trial which is irrelevant to this case. There is no need for us to have to go through all of the documents subsequently if the parties do not wish to rely on them. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If we are clear on this, if that means that in our final submission we can make reference to an exhibit from a previous case that has not been tendered but still make reference to it in the final submission, then that's fine. But that means it will be admitted at the time of the final brief because that's the point at which we evaluate the totality of the evidence and present our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If this means that in the end you will just ask for all documents to be admitted, then we're back to square one.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, we are ridiculing the process at all. We are trying to defend our client, and we're trying to get the evidence that we will need in the end, and we don't know what that is yet. This isn't a case of swamping the Chamber or making a farce of a trial, of course not. It is to be in a position to make submissions based on the trial record. And we say that some of these things may become relevant in 10 months even though they aren't crucial now. But the man has said, he's going to -- he's adopted his statement. Now, there's the example, Your Honour. In a year and a half from now, there may be an argument to be made based on something that this person said in cross on a document. We may have to make that submission, or the Prosecution may have to make that submission. It's not a question of swamping you or clogging the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's hear what Mr. Pantelic has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honours, just for the record the Zupljanin Defence adopts all submissions made by our learned friend Mr. O'Sullivan because during the break we discuss this matter and practically tailored our approach. Just for the record, Your Honour, the spirit of the Rule 92 ter from my point of view is the following: 92 ter rule is actually, how can I say, a Siamese twins. It's a two bodies, two heads in one body because testimony of the witness and the exhibits tendered through that witness in previous transcripts is one body. And at certain stage, now maybe it's not so clear, but at certain stage, it might be very important. I don't see any particular reason, with all due respect, Your Honour, why we cannot have all relevant exhibits tendered in previous proceeding through particular witness and then at the final stage to decide which kind of exhibit we shall make reference. And in addition, Your Honour, please, I don't see in the previous trials in case law of this Tribunal the different approach related to the adoption of a 92 ter previous exhibits tendered through particular witness, and his or her relevant statement. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You will appreciate, Mr. Pantelic, that I mentioned just awhile ago that relevance is the key issue here. And I think the controversy between the Chamber and Mr. O'Sullivan at this moment is that where Mr. O'Sullivan says that all documents are per se relevant, then the Chamber has a different view and thinks that it is still possible to exclude a number of documents from the earlier testimony that are not relevant to this case. But I think enough has been said at this point at the moment. The Chamber will consider it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry, may I just mention something in relation to one of Mr. O'Sullivan suggestions, and that is that all exhibits would come in through the final brief. We would certainly say that wasn't a helpful way of doing it because then we wouldn't know in advance what were admitted exhibits, whether we had anything to say about the admission of the exhibits and the like. Can I say this, and I do support Mr. O'Sullivan on this, in the end you, the Judges, shouldn't be doing the work. We counsel will be saying of the exhibits which have been admitted, now that we've seen the full issues in the case, and part of the problem is we don't yet have a clear idea of what is going to be an issue in the case, we say the following exhibits, whether it's in oral submissions or in the final briefs that we submit, are the relevant ones. So it is our job, as you rightly point out, Your Honours, to indicate from the cadre of documents admitted which are the relevant ones that you should look at. But if they are not admitted at this stage, the stage when the witness comes or whatever, then there's a problem. And so on this, the Defence and Prosecution are completely ad idem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsels, we have to get on with our business and the Chamber has considered the matter once again. The ruling that we gave in -- when we came in after having the break was that the testimony in its entirety goes in, the documents that have been selected by the Prosecution are admitted into evidence, and the Defence is then free to put whichever documents they wish to the witness and have that or those documents admitted into evidence through this witness. And what we will add to this is that if by the end of the cross-examination, and the cross-examination will take place just in the normal fashion, if by the end of the cross-examination and by the end of the witness's testimony the Defence wish to have further documents admitted into evidence, then they will provide a list of those extra documents to the Chamber, and we'll have them admitted. If at a later stage further down the road, the Defence becomes aware of a document that they would still wish to have admitted and that were once admitted in the -- through this witness in the earlier trial, then the bar table motion still remains an available option to the Defence, then Defence is free to at that later stage to seek admission into evidence of this -- into this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It goes without saying that we will still require that whichever document is being sought admitted into evidence must still be relevant to this trial. So there's an underlying and perpetual requirement of relevance. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour -- Your Honour, just one remark. If the Court insists on relevance as the fundamental principle, then the question is why the Court allows 92 ter witnesses at all. You see, where the problem is, when you admit an entire transcript, it's 88 per cent irrelevant to this trial. In other words, out of the evidence of the witness in the previous trial, 88 per cent is irrelevant to us. 12 per cent is relevant. If we admit a whole transcript, then we have to admit all of the documents as well that would be the logical bond because there is a logical bond between the evidence, the transcript that is, and the body of documents. If we admit only part of the documents, then the transcript ultimately will have no purpose. Why accept 92 ter witnesses at all? They should instead come here viva voce, 15 exhibits will be shown to them by one party, 15 by another, and that's the solution to the problem. Because I don't see a logical link between introducing the whole transcript of a witness's evidence from a previous trial and only a certain number of the underlying documents. I say there is really an underlying problem in logics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely agree, Your Honour, just for the record. This is a very, very -- very professional, mindful, and fully in assistance with the judicial economy, Your Honour, this approach, just to swap 92 ter witness to viva voce, be focused on particular issues, and we shall have a clear transcript, we shall have clear list of exhibits which will assist you and the parties here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think this is putting the cart before the horse. While we were discussing during the break, the Judges were considering actually requiring both parties to identify and highlight the relevant parts of the testimony and to do so in advance, to the effect that only those highlighted parts would be admitted. Now, due to the intervention made by Mr. O'Sullivan and in order to not cause any prejudice to the Defence, we ended up allowing the whole testimony to come in. So the reason why we ended up doing that was actually to come forward and meet the requirements of the Defence. But still we think that the requirement of relevance does justify a more careful look at the underlying documents that were admitted in the previous trial through this witness and, as you said yourself, Mr. Zecevic, large parts of the earlier testimony might be irrelevant to this case. For those parts, the Chamber will have to do the work that we still think should be done by the parties. So for the testimonies, we will have to determine which parts of the testimony that are really relevant, and we are assisted in this by the highlights offered by the Prosecution. Those highlights have no legal bearing, they are merely an assistance to the Chamber and we are thankful for that. But still documents that were admitted in the previous trial in parts of the testimony that really, as you say yourself, are irrelevant to this case should not be admitted into this trial. And we have now created a mechanism by which we think that full attention has been given to the demands of the Defence. We ask you to identify documents that you wish to have admitted and that you did not have time to put to the witness while he was here during the cross-examination, and we will admit those documents. And if that is not sufficient, then there is a safety clause in that in the end, by the end of the trial you still have the option of admission of whatever document that is you think should be admitted through the bar table motion. And, you know, I don't think we can do anything more to -- to accommodate the needs of the parties. And as I said, there's an underlying requirement of relevance, so in your own submission, Mr. Zecevic, it seems that a number of the documents that were admitted in the previous trial are not necessarily relevant to this case and should not be admitted. I would like to conclude this discussion now. We have gone long enough, and I think maybe it's even it's time for a break before -- 12.05. Another hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, sit straight through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. And it's about time that we get the witness in. But please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll be very brief. What Ms. Korner said is really the essence. All of this will have absolutely no impact on the workload of the Trial Chamber. Both parties will, in final submissions or in 92 bis submissions, will say that we believe that the transcript of this witness's evidence is relevant in points 72 and 73. The other party will say, No, it's relevant in paragraphs 89 and 91. That is how we will submit to Your Honours what we believe is relevant. But at this moment neither we nor the Prosecution are able do this. And the Defence in particular cannot tie its own hands by showing to the witness exhibits that today seem relevant and may not be relevant at all tomorrow, or maybe in six months because by that time that particular fact will not be in dispute, something else will be in issue. utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was the fifth person brought and another four were brought after me, so we were nine in this small place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.text: I will explain this portion here. See this new large building, it didn't used to be there before because it was recently built. That's why I'm explaining it so that there are no objections later on. And garages used to be there because that was the fence that divided these two perimeters. So from the prison to the garage, this is the area. While this was all construction company site, there were wooden makeshift huts here that belonged to the construction company Dvadeseti Oktobar, the Twentieth of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks, I seek to tender that and one more aerial shot on this which should assist. So I seek to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P421, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we just now have another aerial shot please, P3 -- sorry, 65 ter 341801. Can we focus just a bit further in on the exact centre. Yes, that's fine. Thank you, just like that. Actually, no, can we make it a bit smaller, we need to see more of the bottom. That's probably better. Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just again mark the area where Betonirka garages were and where the cells were that you were kept.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Betonirka garages were here. In this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Just put a letter B next to that, B for Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And just again mark the roof, the roof area of the cells where you were kept.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Again just mark it PC.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And finally on this one, again if you could just mark the roof of the police building.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I seek to tender that. JUDGE HALL. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P422, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: While we are still on geography, can the witness be shown P107, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, this map is not really going to enable you to do anything much more than provide a general indication. But can you show us on that map, if you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if the image can be made a bit bigger, that might be a bit of assistance. That's probably better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you indicate with a dot where the police station was located. Make it as small as possible.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Let me just orient myself. It should be there. Since this here is a football pitch and the stadium, so it should be right next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Given the proximity to Betonirka, I won't ask to you indicate that. One other feature perhaps is Hasan Kikic school, can you show us on the map where that was located.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hasan Kikic school should be somewhere here. It's very hard to show it because the map is on such a small scale. But it should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just mark that, if you would, with the initials HK. Make them small, please.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if it's possible to mark and the map the location of Krings Hall, could you do that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Krings, just a minute, please. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could just write the letter K next to that so that in the future we'll know that that represents Krings Hall.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, we could have a problem here. The witness has marked two things HK.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I thought about that. Your Honours, given that -- yes, I understand what you are driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be safest, could you go back and --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put KR for Krings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. HKR now stands for Krings. HK stands for the Hasan Kikic school. The unmarked dot with no letters next to it on the right represents the police station. And on that basis I seek to tender the image.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P423, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that Betonirka was approximately 50, I think you said 50 to 60, or 50 to 80 metres away, that order of metres. In the time that you were imprisoned in the cells at the police station, did you ever hear anything from the direction of Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 25th of May. Those of us who were in the cell didn't know any longer what was happening outside except that on the 26th, there were a lot of shells falling. On the 27th during the day in the evening and also during the night, we heard that from the Betonirka compound there were the sounds reaching us, the sounds of crying, screaming, blows, and so on. Based on that, we concluded that people were imprisoned there. We didn't know that, we simply heard this. This lasted throughout our entire stay. At certain intervals, at certain times during the day or night one could hear moaning, crying, shouting, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And just lastly on this issue, did the metal plate that was fixed over the window, did that cause problems in audibility?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Given that it was just plain tin sheet and the sounds could reach us through it, we could hear the sound made by military personnel and radio sounds coming from the military building next door. The propaganda programme that was aired on the radio, we could hear it. So we could hear all of the sounds around the prison. The walls are not thick. It's quite a low building, you could see what it looked like. And through the tin sheet, we could hear the sounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add this, some people were in the meantime transferred from Betonirka to our cells. They came with visible injuries. On the other hand, some people were transferred from the cells to Betonirka. So this is how we were able to find out about what had been going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay, thanks for that explanation. Turn now to another topic, you've testified that on the 17th of June, 1992, you were transferred from the prison cell to Manjaca. I want you to cast your mind back to that particular day and I want you to tell that Trial Chamber how that exercise was conducted, how it happened, that you were taken from the cells to Manjaca. The first question I want to ask you is this, who took you out of the cells ready for your trip to Manjaca? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already gave evidence about this. When the cell door was opened assistant chief of police appeared, Drago Vujanic, he had a list. He and another soldier wearing a military uniform appeared. Drago had papers on him, and he was calling out names. Drago and policeman escorted me and another colleague of mine, whose name was called out. Each of us had four policemen escorting us. They had weapons pointed at us. We had to pass through the police station compound with our heads bent down and our hands behind our backs, and we were taken to the back area where the police garages are, and we were taken to the Betonirka compound. Drago Vujovic ordered me to get on the truck there. Since we were colleagues, he is also a lawyer and we were close friends, we went to university together, so I asked him whether he could give me my papers. I was referring to the papers that had been taken out of my pocket, my ID, driver's licence, and so on. And he said, Don't worry, it will reach you subsequently. So we were escorted by police. The police escorted us to Manjaca as well. On the 17th --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Can I just interrupt you there. I just want a few more details but just go --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to interrupt. Maybe my learned friend can clarify with witness the exact family name of this person Drago that he mentioned because it's appeared to me that it's not precise in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just before I do that, though, just before I go back to the transfer, I just want to, I'm sorry about this, but cast your mind back to the period of time when you were still incarcerated in the cells. Very briefly just tell the Trial Chamber during all that time that you were locked up in the police cells, who guarded you and your fellow prisoners? Who was it that guarded you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment we entered the police station perimeter when I was arrested a member of police force asked me to take my belt off, my shoe laces and so on, to empty my pockets, and he took me to a cell. It was the policeman on duty. The same happened to other people. When we were locked in, again we were locked in by a policeman who was on duty that day whom I used to do know, as a former judge and president of the court I knew that policeman, I had known him for many years. The building of that prison was secured by police. They held the keys. And policemen would come once or twice a day to take us out of our cells. They would also bring us food once a day. They also took us for individual questioning. We would be taken to the police administration building and inspectors of the crime prevention police questioned us there, as did members of state security. Therefore, this prison was fully under the jurisdiction of the police and the same applied to other facilities in Sanski Most. Krings, Hasan Kikic school, and all other locations where people were held, all of them were secured by members of the police station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now let's return to the day of your transfer. Firstly, can you clarify for the Defence the name, the surname of the man you mentioned, Drago, was it Vujovic or some other surname?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Vujanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Thank you. All right, now you have told us that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, could you pause about 2 minutes short of the 12.05 adjournment, there are some matters involving the exhibits with which the Registry has to deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, the period that -- you've told us there was the police that took you out of the cells and took you to Betonirka, and you were loaded on to what? Buses or trucks, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was loaded on to a truck which was blue, mid-sized truck. It was driven by a civilian, and we had police escort. Drago Vujanic with several other police inspectors escorted our truck. I also need to add that Drago Vujanic was the prison warden. He was the warden of that prison at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You mean the police cells?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police prison. He was appointed warden of the police prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry to be pedantic, are you talking about the cells where you were kept when you say the police prison?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Those cells and the Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And when you got to Manjaca, who was there to unload you? I don't mean physically, but to oversee the process of you getting off and being herded into your new accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived there and the canvass was lifted off the truck, we were ordered to get off the vehicle. Drago Vujanic held a list, and he called out individual names for us to get off the truck, there were also police inspectors, as I have told you, escorting us whom I also knew. We were then taken over by military police who started immediately mistreating us and beating us. We entered the premises, and they took us to stables all the while terribly beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, if Your Honours, please, that's a discrete. I've got one more topic to go which is a separate issue from this, so would now be an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I was informed by the Prosecution today that two exhibits, mainly Exhibit P366 admitted on the 18th of November, and Exhibit P384 admitted on the 19th of November, should be placed under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So ordered. Before we take the break, there is a brief ruling which the Chamber has to deliver: The Prosecution has sought admission into evidence of around 100 documents through Branko Djeric. In an oral ruling of the 26th of October, 2009, the Chamber determined that it would rule upon the admission into evidence of the documents after the conclusion of the cross-examination of Branko Djeric.
