They are Rule 65 ter numbers 1070, 2877, 2917, 3231, 3237, and 3238. The Chamber has reviewed the testimony of Djeric and the parties submissions as to the admissibility of the remaining Prosecution documents. It finds that the documents are admissible and therefore decides to admit them into evidence. The following exceptions: First, 65 ter number 10135 will not be admitted. And the Chamber does not find that the requirements for -- because the Chamber does not find that the requirements for admission have been met. Secondly, 65 ter number 97 is a duplicate of P179.10. A decision on the admission of the documents the Defence has sought to have admitted through Djeric will be delivered at a later time. So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, thank you for answering questions so far briefly. It's really assisted the Prosecution today, and I would ask that you continue to confine your answers and keep them as brief as possible. Do you know Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Zupljanin well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long time ago. I think it was in 1967, if I'm not mistaken, because that is when I started attending the secondary school of public administration as Banja Luka. I believe that that is where we met, but the gentleman can correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And following that, did you have from time to time professional contact with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I. But that I can explain. So we went to secondary school of public administration. He was one year ahead of me, if I'm not mistaken. We were at the same pupils' accommodation facility, I think, and we socialised and we attended the same faculty and we met there until the end of our studies, and he got a job with the police, whereas I worked in the judiciary and so that we had professional contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. You testified on Friday, 26 April 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, this evidence is at page 5110 of the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You testified that when you are in Manjaca, a number of personalities came to the camp. And you said that the camp was also visited by Stojan Zupljanin and another gentleman, a guy named Nenad Balaban. They were together. Did you also -- did you know this other chap, Nenad Balaban?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is all exactly the way you put it, yes. I knew Mr. Nenad Balaban. He was a judge before the war of the district court at Banja Luka. I believe that for a time he was also the president of the district court of Banja Luka after the war. Now he is attorney at law in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And do you know what role or position or job he had at the time that you saw him in Manjaca? And I'm talking about Balaban now, not Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mr. Balaban's position. I used to meet him even before 1992 while we worked as judges. I remember meeting him when the commander of a reserve JNA unit -- when the -- when there was war in Croatia, and I met him on the territory of the Bosanska Dubica municipality. I found out later that Mr. Balaban was the commander of military security of the 1st Banja Luka Corps of the Serbian army, if I'm not mistaken, that is. But I believe that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified that when you saw both men, Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Balaban, that Mr. Zupljanin was head of the CSB, and that Balaban was dressed in military uniform and Mr. Zupljanin in civilian clothes. Where were you when you first laid eyes on them that day?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Manjaca concentration camp. I was an inmate. It was around lunchtime, we received meals, at the time the meal was served. And I was in the part of the camp where there was a roofed-over place for dining. And Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Balaban passed by, rather, they were passing through the camp, and the commander of the camp, Bozidar Popovic, I think that was his name. I was at that roofed-over place at mealtime, and they went through there and they went to a facility called Konjusnica which means stable. And when they were returning, I decided to speak to them. And I approached them and they stopped and exchanged greetings with me. And this would be the reply to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what was said between you and these two men? What -- how matters proceeded once you had greeted them.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation was very short and so was the encounter. I remember the conversation. The first thing I noticed, especially in Mr. Balaban, was his surprise at my being in the camp. And he said, Are you too in the camp? And then he swore but with no ill intentions. And I said, Yes, I'm here. And he asked about some other colleagues of ours, lawyers, judges, attorneys, who are also Muslims, Bosniaks. And I told him who else there was in the camp, and I asked Mr. Zupljanin, What is all this about? How long is this agony going to last? What will happen to us? And he replied briefly that we would be released, that nothing would happen, so he was telling me that we would all be released from the camp, in a few words. It was a brief encounter. And Mr. Balaban said to me, Well, you are better off here than being in a trench at the front line. And I thought to myself, well, that's probably true. And then they left. And I stayed in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question on this particular topic. You say they went to a facility called Konjusnica which means stable. Were prisoners accommodated or kept in that place, the stable that they went to?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were put up there at the time, I don't recall now. People were put there for a longer time, they were there in isolation. I spent eight days in special treatment that was one group of people, there was another group of people who were ill and isolated for that reason, but I don't remember whether anybody was lying in that part at the time because the stables were actually sufficient as accommodation. I really don't recall whether anybody was in the stable at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you are aware that you've exhausted the hour that you had indicated you would spend on this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours. Can I just seek your indulgence. I'm on my very last topic, and I'm basically just going to show a small excerpt from a video, and that's it. I would estimate I'd probably -- I will be exceeding, but I won't go beyond about 5 to 8 minutes. That sort of order of minutes. It's not going to be a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With leave, Your Honours, just a correction of the transcript. Could my learned friend ask the witness to repeat because one part of his answer when he was speaking about the people who were in the stable, one part of his answer was not recorded. The part when he would have spoke who those people were and why they were put there when he was -- his description of those circumstances didn't make it to the transcript. I cannot suggest to the witness what to say now, but he -- so it may be good for the -- to ask the witness to repeat. Or I'll deal with it in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd prefer it if Mr. Krgovic dealt with it in cross-examination. I'm sure it can be clarified then. Would Your Honours just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just before we move on to the video, you recall in your previous testimony that you described all the various beatings and deaths that occurred in Manjaca that you either learned about from other prisoners or that you saw with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Can the witness be shown P411.40. If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm not quite certain of how to interpret the answer given by the witness to your question because you say -- you asked him whether he recalls in the previous testimony that he described all the various beatings and deaths that occurred in Manjaca that he learned from others or saw with his own eyes. To whom did he describe that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: To the Court. It's in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So he didn't describe it to Mr. Zupljanin or to Mr. Balaban.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm sorry if I made that -- I should have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to clarify. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour is quite right, that's the way I intended that evidence, and I think that is what the witness meant. Very well, is the video ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask for it to stop every now and then, Mr. Draganovic, and ask you to very briefly, again very briefly, comment on what we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, there will be no sound with this excerpt, that's because it's almost inaudible, and for the purposes of this particular witness, there's no need to know what is actually being said. It's actually what you can see that is the relevant testimony. Can we play the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just hold it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of those people? Or have you seen those people before?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to recognise these people now, but I recognise the facility, and I may have seen those people from the camp, but I cannot say this is person X or Y. That's not possible. But this is Manjaca camp. This is the interior of the stable where the people are sitting and the layout as they were placed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just one question, thank you. The disheveled condition of the men that you can see there, was that -- is that how they appeared to you when you first arrived at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified about that in detail in the Brdjanin/Talic case. But I can repeat even now. All of us looked like this then. There was no way we could have been tidy because there were no adequate living conditions there. It's a stable. It's meant for livestock, and staying there for months without the basic living conditions, people cannot look any different from what they look in this image.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we continue playing the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just a watch it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the people in the first scene, and I know the man who was distributing water, and the water bearer. I was in this same stable. So this take shows the inmates distributing water from this plastic container.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I can add that this is stable number 1, the one where I was in. I can tell by the people that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the purposes of the record, I think that's at point 2 minutes, 14.1 second into the tape. Please continue playing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we can see Mr. Ashdown's visit. And we now see Bozidar Popovic the commander of the camp. I don't remember if he was a lieutenant-colonel or a colonel in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Just go back very small. Okay. Now play it. Hold it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, in that particular portion of the videotape which is at 2.23.6, there's a man with military uniform. Who is that? On the left.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the commander of the camp, Bozidar Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we continue playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You can see that gentleman there, he is obviously extremely emaciated and skinny. Did you see any men in that sort of physical condition when you arrived at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most people were in that condition or a similar condition. Those were the early days of the camp when we had been there for up to a month. We can see these journalists are explaining that inmates from Omarska had arrived three days earlier. That is the most difficult time of your stay in the camp because when -- that was a death camp. People were physically mistreated, there was no food, people lived in fear that they would be killed, and so on. So that most people were skinny and everybody had lost weight, 20 kilos or 30. And I'm one of those, I also lost 30 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you say death camp, you are talking about Omarska, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm speaking about the Manjaca camp. The Manjaca camp was a death camp at first, until the international Red Cross came and registered the inmates, and until the UNHCR started supplying the camp with food. So I'm referring to the Manjaca camp not the Omarska camp. Of course the people who had come from Omarska were in an even worse condition than we at Manjaca. We had already heard from the representatives of the International Red Cross that the people at Omarska had been through an even worse ordeal than we at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you could tell by looking at them when they were brought, transported from Omarska, you could see the disastrous condition in which they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we condition playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, I interrupted unnecessarily. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient for my purposes, if Your Honours please, and I'd like to tender that excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. I might have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand that's already in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm sorry, that was -- I was just playing an excerpt, so I didn't need to capture that as a separate exhibit or anything. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, before we leave the picture on the screen, I just have a question about the conditions under which the detainees were held at Manjaca because every time we've seen footages from the stables people have been sitting down in that position. And I think I heard the journalist, the female journalist say, although it was almost inaudible, that they were forced to sit like that for the bulk of the day. And it was only when they were taken out that they could rise. So my question to you is, could you elicit from the witness the conditions for the detainees when they were there, were they allowed to move around freely? Or did they have to sit like this, and for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, you heard His Honour's question, it's clearly put. No need for me to repeat it. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber and clarify that aspect of matters.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I can explain it as follows: In the stables we had to be in one place all the time, either sitting or lying down. Nobody was allowed to leave the stable without special need, so we had to report if we wanted to go to the toilet, and we would be let out in groups of ten with our heads down if we wanted to go to the toilet. Or if we went to do force labour, and daily about 1.000 people went out to do agricultural work or fell trees or build a church, that would be all our movement. Later after several months in the camp, with the permission of the military police, a number of sick people could leave the stable and sit outside, but that would be a group of about 20 or 30 persons. So movement was not allowed. It happened that somebody went out and went to another stable, but if a military policeman noticed -- it happened that I had to crawl from one stable to another, and I was lucky because I wasn't beaten up because I went from one stable to another to see a relative. Once I was hit in the face twice, the military policeman Popovic punched me in the face because we didn't lower our heads when we went toward the stable. He saw us through the wire fence and so I was punched twice and so was my colleague, and we were threatened that we would be taken outside in the evening and beaten. That would be my answer about our stay inside. I spoke in detail in my statement, my earlier statement about the conditions of stay, the conditions that prevailed. And if necessary, I can say more about that. At any rate, the conditions were inhumane. I can say that no one person who was in the camp at which I stayed that didn't suffer serious consequences and who didn't develop an illness, and many inmates have already died at the age of 40 to 50. And I can say that in my assessment that over 500 former inmates of Manjaca camp are already dead. It's not only about the conditions of stay, but also the police officers who kept us there, they were very ingenious in contriving ways of making it more difficult for us. Such as we were made to leave the stables in rainy weather and stand in the rain for hours, and we would then re-enter the stable wet and lie on the concrete floor or the earth floor and of course we were soaked, and the wet clothes would dry on our bodies. Especially in the beginning and also later in the fall, the conditions were utterly inhumane, so there was hardly a person who didn't develop pneumonia or any other serious disease. There was also typhoid fever but that was never published. These people were taken to Banja Luka or some place, I don't know, some people died, others were in a very serious condition. There was a group of people who were seriously ill, they were taken to England, I don't know which month that may have been. And that would roughly be my answer if you are satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. One extra thing briefly, I know that you are anxious to get on, you said that you were kept under special treatment. Can you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said special treatment, you see people who are working military policemen who had access to the camp, they simply had a programme, a plan for torturing us, apart from the beatings, the physical abuse, there was also psychological abuse that I have also mentioned in my evidence. They kept threatening us, telling us that we would never leave the camp alive, that they will kill us. It was a programme followed by military policemen who came into the stables every day and tortured us mentally and physically. That was especially bad in the first half of our stay in the camp. I've already said that this special treatment, or rather part of it, was making us to stand in the rain and, therefore, come back into the stable soaked. And there were many other things, but I've already mentioned them in my prior evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, can I ask a question, we have the images here of the video, do we have the text as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There is a transcript, and we can put it into e-court if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber wishes I'm more than happen happy to put that transcript into evidence. And we can make a note of it and we will attend to it perhaps on Monday or perhaps later during the course of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Two last issues, just very briefly. Was there an Orthodox church, an Orthodox church located anywhere near Manjaca camp that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the Manjaca camp, an Orthodox Christian church was being built. Camp inmates were taken there on a daily basis, escorted by the military police in groups, and the inmates worked for several months on the construction of the church, and the church was built in the time that we were in the camp. It was somewhere above the camp, overlooking the camp. I had never been at that site because I was not one of those people who were allowed to go out. So I don't know exactly, but I think it's 3 to 4 kilometres from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, my last question, which will require me to put to you a portion of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 5453 in the transcript from Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You are asked if civilian police had participated in beatings or whether it was just the military police, and you said this: "On the whole, the military police were involved in the beatings and members of the army. However, in the beatings that took place at night, members of the Serbian police would also participate in them sometimes. The policemen who were providing security in the camp, in particular the Serbian policemen from Kljuc would do this. Some of my cousins from Kljuc were in the camp with me and they were beaten. In the course of the night, they were taken out and both the military policemen and the civilian policemen would beat them. They were given very severe beatings with rifle-butts. They were even beaten, these civilian policemen would even hit them on the fingers with their rifle-butts. They had to put their hands on a table of some sort and then they would hit their fingers with the rifle-butts. "I want to say that the policemen from Sanski Most, the civilian policemen who were providing security, as far as I know they didn't participate in these beatings." Now, how many policemen from Sanski Most were helping out with providing security at Manjaca? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say there were two periods when the civilian police came from Sanski Most on buses to work as security details at the camp. In the first stint they worked there 15 days, and then another 15 days. And they rotated. They came twice from Sanski Most, and I can't remember how many times from Kljuc. But in the beginning of my stay there were policemen from Kljuc there who were particularly cruel to the people, the victims at the camp. That's why I made this distinction because the people from the civilian police force of Sanski Most were people I knew. Some of them were my neighbours. They were working at the police station in Sanski Most and after all is said and done, they were still different from the policemen from Kljuc. One bus load of policemen came the first time, and when they came for another stint, it was again a bus load, 20, 30 men, I don't know exactly. I don't know how many men were needed to guard the camp, but they mostly guarded outside the wire fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my questions. If Your Honours please, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic, I'm appearing on behalf of Mr. Zupljanin, and I have a few questions for you concerning your evidence earlier today and your past evidence in Brdjanin and Talic. Just one thing, we speak the same language and for the interpreters and everyone to be able to follow, we need to make pauses between questions and answers, so after my question, wait for a second or two before you start answering. I'm a fast speaker, you are a lawyer, you will probably answer quickly, we need to be careful. Mr. Draganovic, you mentioned this encounter with Mr. Zupljanin in Manjaca, and from what I understood from your Brdjanin evidence it was in end July, beginning of August; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that it could have been in the second half of the summer. It's hard to say whether it was end July or the beginning of August or the end of August, but it was quite late into the summer. I never noted down that date, and I couldn't be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the only time you saw Mr. Zupljanin in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only time. If he had visited more than that once, I would have certainly heard about it. One the inmates would always spread the news of visitors to the command of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And from what you were able to see, he just passed through the camp, he didn't address anyone with a speech, he didn't hold a rally, nothing like that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there was no speech, and he only passed through the premises of the camp together with the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's this Mr. Balaban; right? He was with him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Balaban was together with Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time when you were held in Manjaca, Zarko Tole an HVO officer captured in combat was also held in Manjaca at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. Mr. Zarko Tole was in the same stable with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was a colleague of Mr. Zupljanin's from before the war, and Mr. Zupljanin visited him on that occasion? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really didn't know that. I don't know anything about the relationship between Mr. Zarko Tole and Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said in your earlier evidence and you mentioned today again that after the arrival of the International Red Cross, and the aid from the UNHCR, the image of Manjaca changed considerably. It was sometime in the summer that these ICRC packages and representatives began to come.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said in my testimony and that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, just one more thing about Manjaca. You said in your evidence that in 1995 when you returned to Sanski Most you found a certain document at the health centre there, a document related to the death of several people during the transportation from Sanski Most to Manjaca, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I found documentation at the health centre in Sanski Most, a list of people who had been transported to Manjaca and brought back from there, including indications of their individual diagnosis. These people were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show a 65 ter document 2786. I'm not sure if it's in this package.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I see an Official Note here where you describe how you found that document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. Could we zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is basically the document you found. You just added a cover letter, this Official Note. I'm not sure if you wrote your note on a separate piece of paper which was then attached or these two were together because we see this here as one document. Could you clarify.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document we see on the screen now is the original document that I found. I wrote an Official Note about this document, and in this Official Note, I explained what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So your note is a separate document basically?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The note is my document, and this is an original that I uncovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the bottom of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The text in bold type. Could the witness read it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The text. Can you read it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the proposal of the Sanski Most court and the Sanski Most Secretariat of the Interior, the examination of the above named was carried out by a medical committee consisting of Dr. Bosko Grubisa and Dr. Stanko Erceg. We established that the above named persons died of asphyxia." Asphyxia, I suppose means suffocation, and here we see the original signatures of Drs. Bosko Grubisa and Stanko Erceg. Between the two signatures we see the stamp of the health centre in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thus, from this document, I get confirmation of your evidence. These people were sent from Sanski Most to Manjaca, and during the journey they suffocated to death and their bodies were taken back to Sanski Most where certain procedures were carried out?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but I'd like to add that among these people who were returned to Manjaca four persons are missing. These people were alive; however, they are not recorded anywhere, nor have they ever been found. It is assumed that they are killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this case the investigating judge issued an order to establish the cause of death, that's what I can see from this document, or that certain steps be taken to find out the cause death.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to follow from what is written here. However, I did not find at the court any sort of protocol written by the investigating judge when I joined the court in 1995. Therefore, this is the only document related to these people that has been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it says here that this was the proposal of the court of Sanski Most and also the SUP, the Secretariat of the Interior of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was up to the police station in Sanski Most and the court of Sanski Most to take steps and procedures to find the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These steps and procedures fell within the jurisdiction of the court and the police in Sanski Most at the time. And we know well that the police and the judiciary at that time were run by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Draganovic. Speaking of the conditions in Manjaca, when you testified in the Brdjanin case, that was on the 22nd of May, when you were shown one document of the charity organisation Merhamet describing the conditions in Manjaca, you said that this report did not reflect the current situation in Manjaca, and you said you thought the reports coming out of Manjaca were not consistent with what was actually happening in those camps, centres.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, and I believe it was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And generally speaking, the people who were responsible, in this case Colonel Popovic or anyone else responsible for any such centre, when they would be sending a report that had been asked, they would always try to look it better than it actually was.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the people in this organisation Merhamet really helped us a lot. They would come from time to time. They would bring some aid that was precious for us camp inmates. Can I go on? But I have to say that these people were under very strict control by General Talic, I believe, directly. And their reports had to be subjected to some sort of censorship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Merhamet was a Muslim humanitarian or charity organisation; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have documents about the establishment of Merhamet, and they show that Merhamet was founded by the Serb authorities. For instance, in Sanski Most, it was the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most who decided who would be in the Merhamet organisation. Now, in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't mean to go into detail. I was just asking for your conclusion that people who were running certain facilities when writing reports to superior authorities always tried to show things looking a little better than they actually were.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I accept that. Moreover, whenever a delegation would be announced or a team of reporters or a visit from a humanitarian organisation, before that visit, inmates would be forced to tidy up a little, throw some quick lime on to dumps, clean up a bit as far as was possible in those conditions to make it look a little better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Your Honour, I forgot. I would like to tender this document. If it's not in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again I understand it's part of the 65 ter package.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about the conditions in Sanski Most and the reports describing that situation, do you know perhaps that Mr. Stojan Zupljanin in the summer of 1992 formed a commission whose job was to tour police stations in Sanski Most, in Prijedor, and Bosanski Novi, to establish the existence or non-existence and the conditions prevailing in such detention facilities, camps, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've seen a document to that effect somewhere, but I really can't remember what was written in it. I think something like that passed through my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You could have seen it when you were reviewing all sorts of documentation in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Draganovic, excuse me. We were a bit late starting today. I need to find the document I want to show you. Meanwhile, let me ask you this: You said you were arrested on 25th May 1992. You said you were arrested by Dane Kajtez, aka Danilusko; Bata Vukic; Vase Davidovic; and Milorad Krunic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think, except I'm not sure about Krunic, I'm not sure I mentioned him, but the other three are correct. Possibly. I don't know. Maybe he was the driver of that Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this man Dane Kajtez, he was a member of the SD Serbian Territorial Defence, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Danilusko Kajtez was a member of the SOS at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you described them at that moment as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They really wore camouflage military uniforms with insignia of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And after that you were taken to the police station and from your explanation I concluded that the place where the cells are is physically separated from the police station, that means some sort of shed or something in the yard; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That facility is part of the police premises, or the public security station premises. Although you are right in saying that it's physically separated from the main building.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, were you able to see this document possibly in 1995 when you returned to Sanski Most or later on?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please give me some time to read it, or you read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read out the parts I'm interested in. I'm interested in some parts only, and I will show you the signature. It says here that: "At Sanski Most during combat activity two centres were established. One of them was the collection centre at the gymnasium, and the other was a collection and investigation centre at the Betonirka factory. On the 1st of August, the gymnasium was vacated ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat his last words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "... and the collection and the investigation centre was established at the Krings Factory Hall. "The Crisis Staff of the municipality ordered their investigation centre to be set up. It made the decision that the prison should be set up the Betonirka company facilities. It appointed the warden and assistant warden of the prison, who were given personnel for physical security. The personnel consisted of members of the former TO and four or five members of the reserve police force." Mr. Draganovic, did you know that a prison warden was appointed, I believe that you spoke about Mr. Dragan Vujanic, or did you say Dragomir?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Drago. And that his assistant was Krunic. Were you familiar with these facts at the time when you were in detention?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just ask that the remainder of the document be shown to me, or that the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the second page to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll go through the entire part that is relevant for the detention, and then I'll ask you a few questions, or if you wish, I can give you a hard copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to have a look at it. I am afraid that I might say something wrong unless I see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the signature but don't say the name, please.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall whether or not I've seen this document in the documentation. If the document was given to the OTP, then I must have seen it. Otherwise, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you whether this was one of the documents that you found when you returned to Sanski Most in 1995.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. It's a document from the Sanski Most police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, I would like to revert you to the first page of the document, and then I will ask you a few questions. But you didn't answer my last question, it follows from this document --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer. Go ahead and ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It follows from this document that the Crisis Staff of the Sanski Most municipality established the prison in Betonirka and the Sports Hall and that a warden and a deputy warden were appointed. Does this correspond to your knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the warden was Drago Vujanic, and his assistant was Krunic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Drago Vujanic, the Crisis Staff appointed a warden Papric, the retired or earlier police chief. I knew that. Papric, I believe his first name is Miladin, and I don't know if he is still alive. He lived in Prijedor. He with Nedeljko Rasuo and two other members of the Crisis Staff from the SDS came to the cell in which I was on the second day after my arrest. And then Papric wore a uniform. He had a police uniform, the uniform of the Serbian police and the uniform of a prison warden. That's when I saw the man, and he said I can see some respectable people here and -- well, I don't have to re-tell it all. But after some weeks or so he was no longer warden, which I learned later on. He soon resigned because he had seen at Betonirka that respected citizens of Sanski Most were being beaten up, and that's why he said that he would -- he didn't want to do his job anymore, if that's sufficient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please look at the -- especially the second page of the document which speaks about the conditions prevailing in what they call collection centres and collection -- and investigation centres. And I will ask you some brief questions about that and you will explain that part of to me later. It says here that these facilities, apart from Betonirka, were lit, that the inmates had blankets, Styrofoam, that they had water, that they were entitled to visit, receiving visits, and inhumane conditions and bad treatment of the inmates isn't mentioned here. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what you have read, but these statements are false.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the one receiving such a report would have no reason to doubt it's content if he receives it from a responsible person?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that the people responsible tried to depict the situation different from what it was; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please accept my previous answer. I don't want to comment this. I cannot say what other people are thinking and how they are going about their duties. I must tell you that there was daily correspondence and special orders going from chiefs of police or circulating among chiefs of police, chiefs of CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you were only detained in police detention on the premises of the police station?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was in the detention facility for only 24 days. It was part of the Sanski Most police station. As president of the municipal court of Sanski Most without a written order, without any investigation, without any document, I was kept in an inhumane conditions and taken to Manjaca concentration camp, and there are documents that show the circumstances of my release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were taken to Manjaca, the vehicle in which you were taken there was escorted by, among others, the warden Vujanic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, he was the commander of the police station, that is the CSB. He was chief at the time, Drago Vujanic, and he was also prison warden. Next to him there was Zoran Despot who was a criminal police inspector at the Sanski Most police station. And there were two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. You said that he was chief of police. When you say so, he was chief of the SJB, the public security station?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't Milan Ivanic chief at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just elicit the answer to this last question, and then I'm finished for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, do you know that at the time Milan Ivanic was commander of the police station?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know there were assistant chiefs of police. I believe that Mr. Ivanic was one of the assistants of the chief of police, and I believe that only in a later period Ivanic became chief, but at the time, as far as I remember, Mr. Drago Vujanic was chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you a document --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't rule out the possibility that due to the lapse of time I might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Draganovic. I have no more further questions of you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, the -- it is regrettable that you are going to be inconvenienced by having to remain with us a few days more. Tomorrow is a UN holiday and the court will not be sitting, and on Monday the court had made previous arrangements not to sit in order to catch up with certain procedural and administrative matters. So, therefore, this trial is now suspended until Tuesday morning. And for the information of counsel, we resume at 9.00 in Courtroom II. So Mr. Draganovic, you are excused as a witness. You are not of course released, and I repeat the usual cautions about not communicating with anyone, and I wish you is safe weekend, and likewise counsel and the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just remind Your Honours that I did make an oral application yesterday in respect of the documents that I didn't manage to get in with the witness who was in closed session. So that perhaps you can deal with it on your -- the day for dealing with administrative matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of December, 2009, at 9.00 at a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
